item.title: Health Ministry reviewing safety for maritime health workers following rescue
item.description: Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa says the Ministry will review the safety measures in place for health workers providing services in maritime areas following concerns raised about the challenges faced by frontline workers. The issue was raised by the media following concerns from medical professionals about the support and safety arrangements for healthcare workers carrying out servi
item.content:encoded:
Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa says the Ministry will review the safety measures in place for health workers providing services in maritime areas following concerns raised about the challenges faced by frontline workers.

The issue was raised by the media following concerns from medical professionals about the support and safety arrangements for healthcare workers carrying out services in maritime communities.

Ravunawa says h ealthcare workers had been providing services for decades and were committed to serving patients and communities, often putting others first while sometimes forgetting to look after themselves.

Responding to questions on whether the ministry was looking into having safer and more suitable boats specifically for maritime health services, Ravunawa says the ministry was definitely looking into the issue.

He says climate change had changed the conditions and challenges faced at sea, and the ministry needed to upgrade its approach to ensure boats used by health workers were safe and provided comfort for staff carrying out maritime services.

Ravunawa says the incident involving six health workers and a boat operator rescued after spending more than 36 hours at sea was a learning opportunity for the ministry.

He acknowledges the resilience of the affected health workers and the medical team in Lakeba, who provided immediate care to those rescued from the water.

Ravunawa expresses his gratitude to Dr Luke and the team for their teamwork, collaboration and professionalism in continuing to provide care while the team awaited the return of the vessel to Lakeba.

He says while the incident highlights challenges, it also showed the positive side of the response through the teamwork and dedication of health workers who provided immediate care throughout the night until the boat docked back at Lakeba.

Responding to questions from the media about concerns that safety was not highlighted in the Ministry of Health’s Strategic Plan 2026–2031, Ravunawa says he would need to go back and review the plan.

He says the concerns raised during the discussion needed to be taken seriously and, if safety measures were not included, the ministry would need to work through policy and legislation to ensure health professionals serving in maritime areas were covered.

Responding to questions from the media about concerns raised by the Fiji Medical Association regarding healthcare worker safety and the availability of a boat specifically for health services, Ravunawa says the affected team from Lakeba Sub-Divisional Hospital was part of the community outreach team providing services across the Southern Lau Group up to Ono-i-Lau.

On the boat used by the affected team, Ravunawa says the health workers were part of the Lakeba Sub-Divisional Hospital’s community outreach team, which provides services across the Southern Lau Group up to Ono-i-Lau.

He says their mode of transport had been a fibre boat fitted with a 75-horsepower engine, operated by a trained captain who had undergone Maritime Safety Authority of Fiji (MSAF) training.

Ravunawa says this arrangement had been used for many years, but during this incident the engine failed, and the team could not control the situation as the boat began taking in water.

item.title: Strong workplace leadership key to improving workers' lives - Singh
item.description: Government can establish sound laws, policies and minimum employment standards, but it is the quality of leadership in our workplaces that transforms these protections into positive everyday experiences for workers. This was highlighted by the Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations , Agni Deo Singh during a talanoa session with teachers in Taveuni.
item.content:encoded:
Government can establish sound laws, policies and minimum employment standards, but it is the quality of leadership in our workplaces that transforms these protections into positive everyday experiences for workers.

This was highlighted by the Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations , Agni Deo Singh during a talanoa session with teachers in Taveuni.

Singh stressed that legislation and policy alone cannot deliver meaningful improvements without strong and innovative leadership in the workplace.

He says innovative leadership is not only about technology or introducing new systems, but also about creating a culture of trust, encouraging new ideas, supporting workers' wellbeing, investing in skills development, and leading with empathy, accountability and integrity.

He says organisations that place workers at the centre of decision-making are more likely to achieve higher productivity, improved staff retention, stronger workplace relationships and sustainable growth.

During the interactive session, teachers discussed a range of employment-related issues, including the minimum terms and conditions of employment, workers' rights, occupational safety and health, and Government initiatives.

The Minister also encouraged school management, employers and managers to adopt modern leadership approaches that promote collaboration, continuous learning, effective communication and workplace wellbeing.

He highlighted the Ministry's ongoing efforts to strengthen Fiji's labour market through the review of employment laws, including the National Minimum Wage and sectoral wages, enhanced workplace compliance, safer working environments, employment creation initiatives and productivity improvement programmes.

He also acknowledged the important role teachers play in shaping Fiji's future workforce, saying they are nurturing the future leaders, innovators and workers who will drive the country's economic and social development.

Cancer stigma and myths are putting children's lives at risk - Ali

item.content:encoded:
Myths and misconceptions about childhood cancer are preventing some children from receiving life-saving treatment, according to WOWS Kids Fiji board member Anabel Ali, who is urging communities to end the stigma surrounding the disease.

Speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, Ali highlighted that the organisation has come across families and communities that discourage or even prevent children diagnosed with cancer from seeking medical treatment.

Ali says while adults have the right to make decisions about their own healthcare, children depend on their parents and caregivers to access treatment.

Ali says delaying or refusing treatment can shorten a child's life and reduce their chances of recovery.

She says there is a misconception that a cancer diagnosis automatically means death, but many children can recover and go on to live normal lives if the disease is detected early and treated promptly.

Ali says WOWS Kids Fiji is currently supporting 64 children battling cancer across Fiji, including 43 boys and 21 girls , with a 10-month-old baby being the youngest child receiving support.

She says they have lost five children since January this year and see around 30 new childhood cancer cases annually.

She adds that the number of children affected by childhood cancer could be even higher, as some cases may be managed directly through hospitals or private healthcare providers.

Ali is urging communities to talk openly about childhood cancer, recognise the early warning signs and encourage families to seek medical attention as soon as possible, saying early diagnosis and access to treatment give children the best chance of survival.

item.title: Tooth decay affecting 8 in 10 five-year-olds in Fiji - Ravunawa
item.description: Almost eight out of every 10 five-year-old children in Fiji are already experiencing tooth decay, with the Ministry of Health reminding children that brushing their teeth twice a day can help protect their health, confidence and future. item.content:encoded:
Almost eight out of every 10 five-year-old children in Fiji are already experiencing tooth decay, with the Ministry of Health reminding children that brushing their teeth twice a day can help protect their health, confidence and future.

Speaking at the National Tooth Brushing Day celebrations at Queen Victoria School, Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa highlighted that oral health has a direct impact on children's daily lives, including their ability to enjoy food, concentrate in class, attend school and smile with confidence.

Ravunawa says by the time students reach the ages of 12 and 15, about half are affected by cavities, while nearly 90 percent of teenagers with tooth decay have not visited a dentist for treatment.

He says poor oral health during childhood can have long-term effects, noting that many older Fijians are missing an average of nine teeth, with some having lost all their natural teeth.

Ravunawa says the Government wants to change this trend by encouraging children to develop good dental habits from an early age.

He says the Ministry of Health, schools and partners such as Colgate-Palmolive are working together to improve children's oral health through dental screening, protective sealants and fluoride treatments.

Ravunawa reminded students that the key message for National Tooth Brushing Day is simple: brush for two minutes, twice a day, once in the morning after breakfast and once at night before going to bed.

He says students should use fluoride toothpaste to help keep their teeth strong and healthy.

He also acknowledged the support of Colgate-Palmolive, saying the company's contribution of toothbrushes and fluoride toothpaste is helping put the power of a healthy smile directly into the hands of Fiji's children.

The Assistant Minister says the Government remains committed to ensuring every child in Fiji, including those living in remote and maritime communities, has access to clean water, toothbrushes and proper dental care.

He encouraged schools, families, communities and corporate partners to work together to ensure every child in Fiji grows up healthy and smiling.
